blocks.md: This lesson follows **Actuator Transmission Limits** in *The Physical Body* (Vol IV).

blocks.source: Vol IV, The Physical Body, § Actuator Transmission Limits
blocks.md: When a policy writes a 50 N·m torque setpoint to a joint register or dispatches an emergency brake command over a Controller Area Network (CAN) bus or EtherCAT, the drive electronics may clamp the current at half that request while returning a clean acknowledgement packet in sub-millisecond time. In digital software, an execution target either accepts an instruction or raises a fault; in physical hardware, stator winding inductance, DC bus voltage headroom, magnetic saturation, and transmission elasticity bound what the joint actually delivers.

blocks.md: Compare your answer with the book's claim: A reduction N multiplies torque by N but reflects rotor inertia by N^2, so acceleration peaks at the inertia-matching ratio and, for a fixed motor and gear, holding heat times reflected inertia does not depend on N.

questions.q: The section **Actuator Transmission Limits** develops one of the chapter's claims. Which one?
options: Compute and drives share one DC bus whose impedance turns a coincident current step into droop toward converter lockout while a regenerative stop pumps energy back, so the permission rail is isolated and held up and every unpowered state is specified.

A reduction N multiplies torque by N but reflects rotor inertia by N^2, so acceleration peaks at the inertia-matching ratio and, for a fixed motor and gear, holding heat times reflected inertia does not depend on N.
Gear compliance and backlash put lost motion and limit cycles between motor and load, so measured motor position is not the load's position.

A torque command is a current that winding inductance and voltage headroom pace and the inverter current limit caps, and a drive can clamp current silently while acknowledging packets, so the safety path must read measured current.
